entry:
Philosophical thought, traditions, and works of the Western world, beginning with the ancient Greek philosophy of the pre-Socratics. The word *philosophy* derives from the Ancient Greek *philosophía*, literally "the love of wisdom." Western philosophy is usually contrasted with other traditions such as [[Eastern philosophy]].

Ancient Western philosophy covered today's philosophical problems and also pure mathematics and natural sciences such as physics, astronomy, and biology; [[Aristotle]] wrote on all of these. The pre-Socratics were interested in cosmology and sought the *arche*, the first principle of the world. [[Thales of Miletus]] identified water as the arche, and his use of observation and reason leads many to call him the first philosopher. [[Pythagoras]] and his followers held that "all is number." Parmenides argued that the world is singular, unchanging, and eternal, while [[Heraclitus]] held that everything is in flux. Empedocles proposed four classical elements, and Leucippus and Democritus proposed atomism. The Sophists, teachers of rhetoric, generally promoted subjectivism and relativism.

The Classical period centers on [[Socrates]] and two generations of students. His critical approach, now called the [[Socratic method]], examined people's views on justice, beauty, truth, and virtue. Socrates wrote nothing himself; his disciples Plato and Xenophon recorded some of his conversations. Tried by the Athenian democracy for impiety and corrupting the youth, he was executed with poison hemlock. [[Plato]] founded the Platonic Academy and, like Socrates, identified virtue with knowledge, raising questions of epistemology.

Later phases include medieval integration of Aristotelian logic with Christian theology, early modern thought, Enlightenment empiricism, and divergence in the 19th and 20th centuries into analytic and continental traditions.

Group of wild and domesticated grasses of the genus *Triticum*, cultivated for their grain, a staple food worldwide. Species and hybrids include the most widely grown [[Common wheat]] (*T. aestivum*), spelt, durum, emmer, einkorn, and Khorasan or Kamut. The archaeological record suggests that wheat was first cultivated in the [[Fertile Crescent]] around 9600 BC.

Wheat is grown on a larger area than any other food crop (219.5 million hectares in 2024), and world trade in it exceeds that of all other crops combined. World production in 2024 was 799 million tonnes, second among cereals after [[Maize|maize]]. Since 1960 production of wheat and other grain crops has tripled.

The plant is a stout, medium to tall grass with a jointed, usually hollow stem. Each flower head holds some 20 to 100 flowers, over 99% of them self-pollinated, and each fertilized carpel develops into a grain. Roots are among the deepest of arable crops, reaching 2 metres.

Hunter-gatherers in West Asia harvested wild wheats for thousands of years before domestication, perhaps as early as 21,000 BC. Repeated harvesting and sowing favored mutant forms with larger grains and a toughened rachis that keeps seeds attached to the ear; as a result, highly domesticated strains cannot survive in the wild.

Wheat is an important source of [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]] and the leading source of vegetable protein in human food, with a protein content of about 13%, relatively high among major cereals but low in protein quality. Gluten, most of its protein, triggers coeliac disease, noncoeliac gluten sensitivity, gluten ataxia, and dermatitis herpetiformis in a small part of the population.

Rotating component, typically circular, intended to turn on an axle bearing. The wheel is a key part of the wheel and axle, one of the six [[Simple machine|simple machines]]. With [[Axle|axles]], wheels allow heavy objects to be moved easily, support loads, and perform work in machines. A wheel reduces [[Friction|friction]] by rolling. Other forms include the ship's wheel, steering wheel, [[Potter's wheel|potter's wheel]], and flywheel.

The English word comes from Old English *hwēol*, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning "to revolve, move around." The wheel probably evolved from rollers, round logs used to move heavy objects. The solid wooden wheel dates to the late Neolithic and appeared alongside the early Bronze Age, after several wheel-less millennia that followed the invention of agriculture and pottery.

The oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement is miniature clay wheels found north of the Black Sea from before 4000 BC. Pictographs of wheeled wagons at the Eanna district of [[Uruk]] date to c. 3500–3350 BC. A potter's wheel from western Ukraine dates to the middle of the 5th millennium BC, earlier than the earliest known use in Mesopotamia. The Ljubljana Marshes Wheel in Slovenia dates to 3340–3030 BC. One recent analysis instead points to copper miners in the Carpathian Mountains, around 3900 BC, as the origin.

The spoked wheel allowed lighter and swifter vehicles. Its earliest known wooden examples are from the Sintashta culture, c. 2000 BC, and horse cultures of the Caucasus soon used spoked-wheel war [[Chariot|chariots]]. Celtic chariots introduced an iron rim in the 1st millennium BC. In China, wheel tracks from around 2200 BC have been found at Pingliangtai, and wheeled vehicles were introduced there from the west.

English playwright, poet, and actor, widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language and the world's pre-eminent dramatist. His extant works, including collaborations, consist of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, 3 long narrative poems, and a few other verses, some of uncertain authorship. His plays have been translated into every major living language and are performed more often than those of any other playwright.

Shakespeare was born and raised in Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover, and Mary Arden. At 18 he married 26-year-old Anne Hathaway; their children were Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith. The years between 1585 and 1592, known as the "lost years," are poorly documented. By 1592 he was part of the [[London]] theatre scene as an actor, writer, and part-owner of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later called the King's Men. Around 1613 he appears to have retired to Stratford.

Most of his known works date from 1589 to 1613. His early plays were primarily comedies and histories. He then wrote mainly tragedies until 1608, among them [[Hamlet]], [[Othello]], [[King Lear]], and [[Macbeth]]. In his last phase he wrote tragicomedies, also called romances, such as *The Winter's Tale* and [[The Tempest]]. His sonnets were published in 1609, and the narrative poems *Venus and Adonis* (1593) and *The Rape of Lucrece* (1594) were his most popular works in his lifetime.

In 1623 fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published the First Folio, a collected edition including 36 plays. Its preface has a poem by [[Ben Jonson]], a rival, who hailed him as "not of an age, but for all time."

Natural movement of air or other gases relative to a planet's surface. Winds range from thunderstorm flows lasting tens of minutes, through local breezes lasting a few hours, to global winds resulting from the difference in absorption of solar energy between climate zones. The study of wind is called anemology.

Wind is caused by differences in [[Atmospheric pressure|atmospheric pressure]], primarily due to temperature differences; air moves from higher to lower pressure. On a rotating planet it is also deflected by the [[Coriolis force|Coriolis effect]], except exactly on the equator. The two major drivers of large-scale [[Atmospheric circulation|atmospheric circulation]] are differential heating between the equator and the poles and the planet's rotation. Thermal lows over terrain can drive [[Monsoon|monsoon]] circulations, and sea and land breezes define local winds on coasts.

Wind direction is the direction from which it originates, so a westerly wind blows from the west. Weather vanes and windsocks indicate direction, and speed is measured by anemometers, most commonly with rotating cups or propellers. Short bursts are gusts, and strong winds of around one minute are squalls; long-duration winds are named by average strength, such as breeze, gale, storm, and hurricane.

In outer space, the [[Solar wind|solar wind]] is the movement of gases or charged particles from the Sun, and planetary wind is the outgassing of light elements from an atmosphere. The strongest observed winds in the Solar System are on Neptune and Saturn.

Wind shapes landforms through aeolian processes such as erosion and the formation of loess, spreads wildfires, and disperses seeds. Humans have used it for sailing ships, hot air balloons, and as a source of [[Wind power|power]].

Use of wind energy to generate useful work, today mostly electricity. Historically used by sails, windmills, and windpumps, it is now generated almost completely by [[Wind turbine|wind turbines]], generally grouped into wind farms and connected to the [[Electrical grid|electrical grid]].

Wind supplied about 2,700 TWh of electricity in 2025, over 8% of world electricity. About 100 GW was added during 2021, mostly in [[China]] and the United States, and global installed capacity exceeded 800 GW. In 2024, 30 countries generated more than a tenth of their electricity from wind, and generation has nearly tripled since 2015.

The power in moving air is proportional to the cube of wind speed, so available power increases eightfold when speed doubles. A turbine's theoretical efficiency is capped at 59.3% by the Betz limit. Almost all large turbines share one design: a horizontal-axis machine with an upwind rotor of 3 blades on a nacelle atop a tall tubular tower. Turbines in a farm are linked by a medium-voltage system, often 34.5 kV, and a substation [[Transformer|transformer]] raises the voltage for transmission.

Supporters describe wind as renewable, with a much smaller environmental impact than burning [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]] and among the lowest costs per unit of energy; in many locations new onshore wind farms are cheaper than new coal or gas plants. Because output is variable, a reliable supply needs energy storage or dispatchable generation. Onshore farms have a greater visual impact than most other power stations per energy produced; offshore farms have less but generally cost more. Critics also cite wildlife effects, including bird and bat collisions. Wind output is often higher at night and in winter, when [[Solar power|solar]] output is low.

Salzburg-born composer and musician of the Classical period. He completed more than 800 works, including outstanding examples of most genres of his time: symphonies, [[Concerto|concertos]], [[Chamber music|chamber music]], [[Opera|opera]], and choral music. He is regarded as one of the greatest composers in Western music.

Born in [[Salzburg]], then within the [[Holy Roman Empire]], Mozart was the youngest of seven children, five of whom died in infancy. He emerged as a child prodigy under his father Leopold, an experienced teacher. At five he was competent on keyboard and violin, had begun to compose, and had performed before European royalty. His father took him on a grand tour of Europe and then three trips to Italy. At 17 he was a musician at the Salzburg court. A fruitless search for employment (1777–1779) took him to Paris, Mannheim, and Munich; during this time he wrote his five violin concertos, and the opera *Idomeneo*.

In 1781, while visiting Vienna, his quarrels with his Salzburg employers came to a head and he was dismissed. He remained in Vienna for the rest of his life, achieving fame and some financial success but no long-term security. He married Constanze Weber on August 4, 1782, and was appointed chamber composer to Emperor [[Joseph II]] in 1787.

His early Vienna years produced the opera *Die Entführung aus dem Serail*, the Great Mass in C minor, and he wrote more than a dozen piano concertos there, many considered masterpieces. In his final years he composed his last three symphonies, culminating in the *Jupiter*, the serenade *Eine kleine Nachtmusik*, the operas *Le nozze di Figaro*, [[Don Giovanni]], *Così fan tutte*, and *Die Zauberflöte*, and the Requiem, largely unfinished at his death at 35.

Adult female human. Before adulthood, a female child or adolescent is called a [[Girl|girl]].

Anatomically, female characteristics of human sexual dimorphism center on the [[Female reproductive system|reproductive system]], which includes the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, vagina, and vulva. Common accompanying characteristics are larger breasts, a generally wider pelvis, less facial and body hair, higher body fat, shorter stature, and less muscle mass; these facilitate pregnancy, childbirth, and breastfeeding. Women typically inherit a pair of X chromosomes. All embryos have female-type genitalia until week 6 or 7, when the SRY gene on the Y chromosome directs a male embryo's gonads to become testes.

Definitions differ in emphasis. Some sources define sex as binary and set by the type of gamete produced, large ova in females, and treat rare disorders of sex development as anomalies. Others note that transgender women were assigned male at birth and that some women are intersex. Since the 1970s, social scientists have increasingly distinguished sex from gender and stressed the social construction of gender.

In [[Puberty|puberty]], signals from the pituitary gland lead the ovaries to secrete hormones that stimulate body growth, breast development, and menarche, the onset of [[Menstruation|menstruation]], which occurs on average at age 12–13. Age 18 is frequently the age of majority.

The English word evolved from Old English *wīfmann*, in which *mann* meant "person"; after the Norman Conquest *man* came to mean "male human." Its supposed connection to *womb* is a misconception.

Women have occupied positions at every level of society, though patriarchal gender roles have often limited them. Feminist movements aim at [[Gender equality|gender equality]].

Natural lignocellulosic material derived primarily from the secondary xylem of trees and other woody plants. In living plants it provides mechanical support and, in the functional sapwood, conducts water and dissolved minerals. It is a natural composite of [[Cellulose|cellulosic]] fibers, strong in tension, embedded in a matrix of lignin and hemicelluloses that resists compression. Dry wood is roughly 40–50% cellulose, 20–35% hemicelluloses, and 15–35% lignin.

A tree's diameter increases by secondary growth: cell division in the [[Vascular cambium|vascular cambium]] adds layers that envelop the whole stem, branches, and roots. Where seasons are distinct, growth appears as rings; the part of a ring formed early in the season is usually lighter, called earlywood, and the later part is latewood. Softwoods, from conifers, are dominated by tracheids, while hardwoods have vessel elements for water transport. Density ranges from about 0.20 g/cm³ in balsa to over 1.0 g/cm³ in lignum vitae.

The earliest known plants to have grown wood, found in New Brunswick in 2011, lived approximately 395 to 400 million years ago. Humans have used wood since prehistoric times for [[Fuel|fuel]], tools, weapons, and shelter, and later for [[Construction|construction]], [[Furniture|furniture]], and [[Paper|paper]]. The earliest spears were crafted from wood, and Neolithic European longhouses were built primarily of wood. Known wooden constructions date back ten thousand years.

Forests worldwide hold a growing stock of about 630 billion cubic metres, and almost 4 billion cubic meters of wood were harvested in 2023, mostly for furniture and building construction. Wood science emerged as a distinct field in the early 20th century.

Basic element of language that carries meaning, can be used on its own, and is uninterruptible. Speakers usually have an intuitive grasp of what a word is, but linguists have no consensus on a definition, and attempts to find specific criteria remain controversial. Some linguists propose avoiding the term in favor of better-defined ones such as morphemes.

A word is distinguished from a [[Morpheme|morpheme]], the smallest unit of language with meaning, even if it cannot stand alone. Words consist of at least one morpheme. In English they generally include at least one root (*rock*, *god*, *write*) and possibly affixes (*-s*, *un-*, *-ly*, *-ness*). Words with more than one root, such as *typewriter*, are compound words.

Definitions can be consistent at particular levels. Phonologically, a word is the smallest segment of sound that can be isolated by word accent and boundary markers. Orthographically, it is a segment set off by blank spaces. Morphologically, it is the basic element of grammatical paradigms such as inflection. Semantically, it is the smallest relatively independent carrier of meaning in a lexicon, and in [[Syntax|syntax]], the smallest permutable and substitutable unit of a sentence. In some languages these types coincide; in others they correspond to elements of different size.

Phonological words can differ from intuition. In Walmatjari, an Australian language, a phonological word must have at least two syllables. The Finnish compound *pääkaupunki* "capital" counts as two phonological words because it does not conform to Finnish vowel harmony within words.

Dictionaries list a language's lexicon as lemmas, indicating what its writers regard as words.
